rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites acknowledged God but worshipped the calf through an interpretive rationale like that used by idol worshippers, so Moses could address them this way.
rows.anchor: أنهم كانوا معترفين بالإله لكنهم عبدوا العجل على التأويل الذي يذكره عبدة الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the good promise as the Torah, which would teach law and give the Israelites distinction among people.
rows.anchor: أن المراد ما وعدهم من إنزال التوراة عليهم ليقفوا على الشرائع والأحكام ويحصل لهم بسبب ذلك مزية فيما بين الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the good promise as God's truthful promise of reward for obedience.
rows.anchor: أن الوعد الحسن هو الوعد الصدق بالثواب على الطاعات

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads the promise as the covenant, specifically God's warning not to transgress and incur His anger; Moses' next question recalls that warning.
rows.anchor: الوعد هو العهد وهو قول مجاهد وذلك العهد هو قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise could cover religious benefits—guidance through scripture and reward—or worldly benefits, including the land and homes of Pharaoh's people, which God gave them.
rows.anchor: الوعد الحسن ههنا يحتمل أن يكون وعدا حسنا في منافع الدين وأن يكون في منافع الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The long covenant may mean the time since God's favors, including rescue from Pharaoh; the phrase also echoes the hardening caused by a long lapse of time.
rows.anchor: أفطال عليكم العهد بنعم الله تعالى من إنجائه إياكم من فرعون وغير ذلك من النعم

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: A report says they mistook forty nights for twenty by counting each day as a night; al-Qadi dismisses this as implausible.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي : هذا ركيك لأن ذلك لا يكاد يشتبه على أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Moses promised thirty nights, then God added ten, making the wait seem long.
rows.anchor: موسى عليه السلام وعدهم ثلاثين ليلة فلما زاد الله تعالى فيها عشرة أخرى كان ذلك طول العهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one literally wants divine wrath; since sin causes it, willing its cause counts as willing its effect indirectly.
rows.anchor: ولكن المعصية لما كانت توجب ذلك ، ومريد السبب مريد للمسبب بالعرض صح هذا الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording supports treating divine wrath as an attribute of action, since an attribute of God's essence cannot descend into a body.
rows.anchor: الغضب من صفات الأفعال لا من صفات الذات لأن صفة ذات الله تعالى لا تنزل في شيء من الأجسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' reference to a broken appointment shows that he had made an appointment with his people; the source announces two explanations but supplies none here.
rows.anchor: هذا يدل على موعد كان منه عليه السلام مع القوم وفيه وجهان

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj prefers reading the verb in the indicative, understanding the phrase as saying it would not return, like the construction in 5:71.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : الاختيار أن لا يرجع بالرفع بمعنى أنه لا يرجع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb is also read in the subjunctive, with أن governing it.
rows.anchor: وقرىء بالنصب أيضا على أن أن هذه هي الناصبة للأفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage establishes the duty to reason about knowledge of God, as do the arguments against worshipping the calf in 7:148 and 7:195.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تدل على وجوب النظر في معرفة الله تعالى وقال في آية أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument does not imply that a speaking calf would be divine: absence of one among many necessary conditions disproves divinity, while its presence alone would not establish it.
rows.anchor: وليس المقصود من هذا أن العجل لو كان يكلمهم لكان إلها لأن الشيء يجوز أن يكون مشروطا بشروط كثيرة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In a reply to a Jewish interlocutor who asked why Muslims differed before burying their Prophet, Ali said Muslims differed about him, while Israelites asked Moses for an idol immediately after crossing the sea.
rows.anchor: فقال : إنما اختلفنا عنه وما اختلفنا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The land is described as a qāʿ, meaning a low, level place; another gloss takes it as a place where water collects.
rows.anchor: كونها قاعا وهو المكان المطمئن وقيل مستنقع الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣafṣaf means ground without vegetation; Abu Muslim glosses both qāʿ and ṣafṣaf as smooth, level land.
rows.anchor: الصفصف وهو الذي لا نبات عليه

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf distinguishes ʿiwaj with kasra for abstract things from ʿawaj with fatḥa for physical things.
rows.anchor: قد فرقوا بين العوج والعوج فقالوا : العوج بالكسر في المعاني والعوج بالفتح في الأعيان

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Although earth is physical, the kasra is apt because minute irregularities invisible to the eye emerge under geometric measurement and are treated like abstractions.
rows.anchor: فإذا قابلتها المقاييس الهندسية وجدت فيها أنواعا من العوج خارجة عن الحس البصري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse indicates that the earth will then be a true sphere, since a polygon's joined faces would meet with curvature rather than straightness.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تدل على أن الأرض تكون ذلك اليوم كرة حقيقية لأن المضلع لا بد وأن يتصل بعض سطوحه بالبعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amt means a slight protrusion; an idiom says to stretch a rope until no such unevenness remains.
rows.anchor: الأمت النتوء اليسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taken together, the four descriptions make the land smooth, with no rises, hollows, deviations, or bends.
rows.anchor: وتحصل من هذه الصفات الأربع أن الأرض تكون ذلك اليوم ملساء خالية عن الارتفاع والانخفاض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view identifies the caller as the trumpet blast; its call turns aside from no one because all are gathered.
rows.anchor: أن ذلك الداعي هو النفخ في الصور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view has a caller on the Jerusalem rock summon the scattered, decayed bodies to judgment; it is said to be Israfil standing on the rock.
rows.anchor: أنه ملك قائم على صخرة بيت المقدس ينادي ويقول : أيتها العظام النخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the summons informs its hearers, it must come after resurrection, since calling the dead would be pointless; if it serves another purpose, such as benefiting angels, it may precede resurrection.
rows.anchor: إن كان المقصود بالدعاء إعلامهم وجب أن يكون ذلك بعد الإحياء لأن دعاء الميت عبث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that terror makes the voices subdued and faint, leaving only a quiet, hidden utterance.
rows.anchor: خشعت الأصوات من شدة الفزع وخضعت وخفيت فلا تسمع إلا همسا وهو الذكر الخفي

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim says humans and jinn recognize God as their sole master, so only a whisper remains, almost too faint to understand except by moving the lips.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم : وقد علم الإنس والجن بأن لا مالك لهم سواه فلا يسمع لهم صوت يزيد على الهمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person facing God's judgment rightly lowers the gaze, weakens the voice, falters in speech, and suffers prolonged grief.
rows.anchor: وحق لمن كان الله محاسبه أن يخشع طرفه ويضعف صوته ويختلط قوله ويطول غمه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وعكرمة وابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrima, and Ibn Zayd interpret hems as the sound of feet moving toward the gathering place.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما والحسن وعكرمة وابن زيد : الهمس وطء الأقدام

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf allows man to be nominative as an apposition to intercession with an omitted genitive, or accusative as its object.
rows.anchor: من يصلح أن يكون مرفوعا ومنصوبا فالرفع على البدل من الشفاعة بتقدير حذف المضاف إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers the accusative because it needs neither ellipsis nor a change in case, refers the exception to beneficiaries, and avoids the obvious claim that an intercessor must be authorized and approved.
rows.anchor: الاحتمال الثاني أولى لوجوه

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila argue that a grave sinner is not approved by God, so the Prophet cannot intercede for him if the verse requires the beneficiary to be approved.
rows.anchor: قالوا : الفاسق غير مرضي عند الله تعالى فوجب أن لا يشفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi calls this among the strongest proofs for intercession for grave sinners: God may approve one of a sinner's utterances, namely the testimony of faith, making intercession beneficial.
rows.anchor: الفاسق قد ارتضى الله تعالى قولا واحدا من أقواله وهو : شهادة أن لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although an objection demands both permission and approval, approval suffices for the exception because 21:28 says intercession is only for one God approves; together the verses establish both conditions.
rows.anchor: هذا القيد وهو أنه رضي له قولا كاف في حصول الاستثناء

none: Qur'an text only; no commentary point in this segment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'this is a message' points to the surah's accounts, promises, threats, and admonitions; balāgh is sufficiency and what brings one to the desired end.
rows.anchor: فقوله هذا إشارة إلى المذكور في هذه السورة من الأخبار والوعد والوعيد والمواعظ البالغة والبلاغ الكفاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some gloss worshippers as learned and others as doers; the best reading combines knowledge and action, since knowledge is a tree and action its fruit.
rows.anchor: الأولى أنهم الجامعون بين الأمرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is a mercy in religion: sent amid ignorance and the confusion of the scriptural communities, he called people to truth, explained the path to reward, legislated, and distinguished lawful from forbidden.
rows.anchor: فدعاهم إلى الحق وبين لهم سبيل الثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People benefit from this mercy when they seek truth rather than cling to imitation, obstinacy, or pride, with divine guidance accompanying them.
rows.anchor: من كانت همته طلب الحق فلا يركن إلى التقليد ولا إلى العناد والاستكبار وكان التوفيق قرينا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was also a worldly mercy because his religion freed people from much humiliation, fighting, and war.
rows.anchor: تخلصوا بسببه من كثير من الذل والقتال والحروب ونصروا ببركة دينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To the objection that the sword and taking property contradict mercy, one answer is that force targets arrogant, obstinate opponents; even divine mercy coexists with punishment, and blessed rain can cause damage.
rows.anchor: إنما جاء بالسيف لمن استكبر وعاند ولم يتفكر ولم يتدبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second answer contrasts earlier prophets, whose rejecting peoples were destroyed, with Muhammad's community, whose punishment was delayed until death or resurrection.
rows.anchor: كل نبي قبل نبينا كان إذا كذبه قومه أهلك الله المكذبين بالخسف والمسخ والغرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection from verses about fighting and punishment is answered by noting that specification of a general rule does not invalidate it.
rows.anchor: لأنا نقول تخصيص العام لا يقدح فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's excellent character itself manifests mercy, as stated in the verse about his immense character.
rows.anchor: نهاية حسن الخلق قال تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that when asked to pray against the polytheists, the Prophet replied that he was sent as mercy, not as punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: A report from Hudhayfa has the Prophet ask that any insult or curse he uttered in human anger be made a prayer for its recipient on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: في رواية حذيفة : ( إنما أنا بشر أغضب كما يغضب البشر

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد
rows.claim: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd limits 'mercy to the worlds' to believers.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الرحمن بن زيد

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم الأنصاري
rows.claim: Al-Ansari says the views converge: the Prophet was mercy for everyone who reflected on God's and His Messenger's signs, while those who turned away brought trial upon themselves.
rows.anchor: والقولان يرجعان إلى معنى واحد

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila argue that if God intended disbelievers' rejection and created their disbelief, the mission would be punishment rather than mercy, contrary to the verse.
rows.anchor: لو كان الله تعالى أراد من الكافرين الكفر ولم يرد منهم القبول من الرسول

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: They reject delayed punishment as the explanation for mercy: worldly benefits existed before the Prophet, and after his arrival fear and fighting harmed many disbelievers.
rows.anchor: بل كانت نعمهم في الدنيا قبل بعثته أعظم لأن بعد بعثته نزل بهم الغم والخوف منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi replies that God knew Abu Lahab would never believe, so commanding him to believe would imply commanding the impossible and turning divine knowledge into ignorance; mission can still be mercy even if God creates disbelief.
rows.anchor: لما علم الله سبحانه وتعالى أن أبا لهب لا يؤمن ألبتة وأخبر عنه أنه لا يؤمن كان أمره إياه بالإيمان أمرا يقلب علمه جهلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a disbeliever's capacity allows only disbelief, the objection follows; if it allows both alternatives, choosing between them requires a divine determiner, so the objection returns.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت صالحة للضدين توقف للترجيح على مرجح من قبل الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mission may be mercy for disbelievers through postponement of total destruction; the verse does not require mercy to operate on the same basis for everyone.
rows.anchor: لم لا يجوز أن يكون رحمة للكافر بمعنى تأخير عذاب الاستئصال عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects the claim that worldly favors explain the mercy: although those favors predated the mission, the Prophet's presence stopped threatened punishment, which was mercy for disbelievers.
rows.anchor: فلما اندفع ذلك عنهم بسبب حضوره كان ذلك رحمة في حق الكفار

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila infer that Muhammad is superior to angels because angels belong to the worlds and he is mercy to the worlds.
rows.anchor: قالوا : لأن الملائكة من العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi counters that angels seek forgiveness for believers and bless the Prophet, who is himself among the believers, so angelic mercy also reaches him.
rows.anchor: والرسول عليه السلام داخل في المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After proving God's oneness and the Prophet's mercy, the passage turns to warning and justifying the command to fight the opponents.
rows.anchor: أتبع ذلك بما يكون إعذارا وإنذارا في مجاهدتهم والإقدام عليهم

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf explains that innamā can restrict either a predicate to its subject or a subject to its predicate; both constructions occur here.
rows.anchor: إنما يقصر الحكم على شيء أو يقصر الشيء على حكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The combined constructions confine the revelation to affirming God's oneness; the question 'will you submit?' calls for pure monotheism and permits proving it through revelation.
rows.anchor: وفائدة اجتماعهما الدلالة على أن الوحي إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم مقصور على إثبات وحدانية الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent implication that only monotheism was ever revealed is false; the restriction is rhetorical emphasis.
rows.anchor: المقصود منه المبالغة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf derives ādhana from 'to know' but says it commonly functions as a warning, as in the declaration of war in 2:279.
rows.anchor: آذن منقول من أذن إذا علم ولكنه كثر استعماله في الجري مجرى الإنذار

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim reads 'I have warned you equally' as openly inviting them to war, making clear Quraysh receive the same treatment as other unbelievers.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم : الإيذان على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the Prophet conveyed equally what the people owed in monotheism and other duties, removing any excuse that no messenger had come.
rows.anchor: فقد أعلمتكم ما هو الواجب عليكم من التوحيد وغيره على السواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation takes 'equally' to mean openly and publicly.
rows.anchor: على سواء على إظهار وإعلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation means that the Prophet will not rush into war but will allow time in hope that they accept Islam.
rows.anchor: والمراد أني لا أعاجل بالحرب الذي آذنتكم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes the unknown timing as the Day of Judgment or worldly punishment; a claimed abrogation by 21:97 is rejected because a report of this kind cannot be abrogated.
rows.anchor: من يوم القيامة ، ومن عذاب الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view refers to the coming war: the Prophet knows it will occur but not when, which shows the surah is Meccan and the fighting command came after migration.
rows.anchor: الذي آذنهم فيه من الحرب لا يدري هو قريب أم بعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view refers to Muslim victory and the disbelievers' humiliation: it is certain, but God did not disclose when it would happen.
rows.anchor: ما يوعدون به من غلبة المسلمين عليهم كائن لا محالة ولا بد أن يلحقهم بذلك الذل والصغار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's knowledge of public and hidden speech commands sincerity and avoidance of hypocrisy, since people should be sincere before one who knows their thoughts.
rows.anchor: فالمقصود منه الأمر بالإخلاص وترك النفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says the possible trial and temporary enjoyment refer to delaying punishment.
rows.anchor: لعل تأخير العذاب عنكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another says the unknown date of punishment tests whether they repent and turn back from disbelief.
rows.anchor: لعل إبهام الوقت الذي ينزل بكم العذاب فيه فتنة لكم أي بلية واختبار لكم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets their present worldly life as a trial, with fitna meaning affliction and testing.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : لعل ما أنتم فيه من الدنيا بلية لكم والفتنة البلوى والاختبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats the delay of fighting as a test if they persist in disbelief; the Prophet says he does not know because they might believe, making their reprieve mercy instead.
rows.anchor: لعل تأخير الجهاد فتنة لكم إذا أنتم دمتم على كفركم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A final reading takes the clarification and warning itself as a trial: refusing after repeated explanation increases punishment, and worldly enjoyment becomes evidence against them.
rows.anchor: لعل ما بينت وأعلمت وأوعدت فتنة لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse has several readings: 'say, my Lord, judge' with kasra, with ḍamma, as 'my Lord is more decisive,' or as a form from iḥkām.
rows.anchor: قرىء : قل رب أحكم بالحق على الإكتفاء بالكسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation asks God to judge between the Prophet and his people through punishment for those who rejected him.
rows.anchor: أي ربي اقض بيني وبين قومي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God ordered the Prophet to follow earlier prophets in this prayer; they asked God to judge justly, and the disbelievers were killed at Badr.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : أمره الله تعالى أن يقتدي بالأنبياء في هذه الدعوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation asks God to separate the Prophet and his opponents in a way that makes the truth visible to all, by granting him victory.
rows.anchor: افصل بيني وبينهم بما يظهر الحق للجميع وهو أن تنصرني عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of the closing phrase invokes God against their descriptions of shirk, disbelief, falsehood, and attacks on the Prophet's call; Ibn ʿAmir reads 'they describe,' addressing believers and asking God's help to refute them.
rows.anchor: من الشرك والكفر وما تعراضون به دعوتي من الأباطيل والتكذيب

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir reads the verb with yāʾ, so the believers are told that God is their aid against what the disbelievers describe falsely.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر بالياء المنقوطة من تحت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says God defeated the opponents' expectation of supremacy by supporting the Prophet and believers and humiliating them.
rows.anchor: كانوا يطمعون أن تكون لهم الشوكة والغلبة فكذب الله ظنونهم وخيب آمالهم

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi says the surah closes with this prayer because the Prophet had fully explained the truth while opponents persisted in abuse and denial; it consoles him to entrust judgment to God, whether punishment comes through fighting or later.
rows.anchor: كان قد بلغ في البيان الغاية لهم وبلغوا النهاية في أذيته وتكذيبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report that the Prophet used this prayer in battles suggests God commanded it to urge him toward fighting them; delayed punishment remains near in certainty.
rows.anchor: وما روي أنه عليه السلام كان يقول ذلك في حروبه كالدلالة على أنه تعالى أمره أن يقول هذا القول

none: Surah heading and Qur'an text only; no commentary point in this segment.
